claim: Spinal circuits generate rhythmic movements.
source: When spinal circuits generate rhythmic movements it is important that the neuronal activity remains within stable bounds to avoid saturation and to preserve responsiveness.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a premise for the study.

claim: Neuronal activity must remain within stable bounds to avoid saturation and preserve responsiveness during rhythmic movements.
source: When spinal circuits generate rhythmic movements it is important that the neuronal activity remains within stable bounds to avoid saturation and to preserve responsiveness.
evidence: This is stated as a functional requirement in the abstract.

claim: Hundreds of neurons were simultaneously recorded from lumbar spinal circuits of turtles.
source: Here, we simultaneously record from hundreds of neurons in lumbar spinal circuits of turtles and establish the neuronal fraction that operates within either a 'mean-driven' or a 'fluctuation–driven' regime.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a methodological approach.

claim: Fluctuation-driven neurons have a supralinear input-output curve.
source: Fluctuation-driven neurons have a 'supralinear' input-output curve, which enhances sensitivity, whereas the mean-driven regime reduces sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The supralinear input-output curve enhances sensitivity in fluctuation-driven neurons.
source: Fluctuation-driven neurons have a 'supralinear' input-output curve, which enhances sensitivity, whereas the mean-driven regime reduces sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is a theoretical prediction tested in the study.

claim: The mean-driven regime reduces sensitivity.
source: Fluctuation-driven neurons have a 'supralinear' input-output curve, which enhances sensitivity, whereas the mean-driven regime reduces sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a contrast to the fluctuation-driven regime.

claim: There is a rich diversity of firing rates across the neuronal population reflected in a lognormal distribution.
source: We find a rich diversity of firing rates across the neuronal population as reflected in a lognormal distribution and demonstrate that half of the neurons spend at least 50 % of the time in the 'fluctuation–driven' regime regardless of behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2F and 9.

claim: Half of the neurons spend at least 50% of the time in the fluctuation-driven regime regardless of behavior.
source: We find a rich diversity of firing rates across the neuronal population as reflected in a lognormal distribution and demonstrate that half of the neurons spend at least 50 % of the time in the 'fluctuation–driven' regime regardless of behavior.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 10.

claim: The disparity in input-output properties between the two regimes may reflect a fine trade-off between stability and sensitivity to maintain flexibility across behaviors.
source: Because of the disparity in input–output properties for these two regimes, this fraction may reflect a fine trade–off between stability and sensitivity in order to maintain flexibility across behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Rhythmic movements such as walking, scratching, chewing and breathing consist of a recurrent sequence of activity generated by neuronal networks primarily in the spinal cord and medulla.
source: Rhythmic movements, such as walking, scratching, chewing and breathing, consist of a recurrent sequence of activity, which is generated by neuronal networks primarily in the spinal cord and medulla.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background knowledge.

claim: Distinct motor tasks have been reported to be divided among dedicated microcircuits in zebrafish.
source: Distinct motor tasks have been reported to be divided among dedicated microcircuits in zebrafish (Ampatzis et al., 2014; Bagnall and McLean, 2014; Fetcho and McLean, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: An arrangement with a spectrum of different firing rates could be beneficial by adding the possibility of increasing the overall activity during uphill walking where a stronger force is needed.
source: An arrangement with a spectrum of different firing rates could be beneficial by adding the possibility of increasing the overall activity, for instance during uphill walking where a stronger force is needed.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction.

claim: Weak stimuli are amplified whereas strong stimuli are attenuated in order to reduce saturation in sensory processing.
source: In sensory processing, neural circuits must be able to retain sensitivity both to weak and strong input. Weak stimuli are amplified whereas strong stimuli are attenuated in order to reduce saturation.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the introduction.

claim: If there is too much activity, the circuit reaches saturation and loses the ability to resolve differences in sensory input.
source: If there is too much activity, the circuit reaches saturation and therefore loses the ability to resolve differences in sensory input.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of excessive activity.

claim: Amplification of weak signals by recurrent excitation poses the risk of unstable activity.
source: Furthermore, amplification of weak signals by recurrent excitation pose the risk of unstable activity, which can spin out of control (Vogels et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Local excitation is carefully balanced by inhibition to assure stability and to widen the range of operation in cortical networks.
source: Stability has primarily been investigated in cortical networks and much evidence suggest that local excitation is carefully balanced by inhibition to assure stability and to widen the range of operation (Galarreta and Hestrin, 1998; Shu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Unstable states such as epileptiform activity can easily be achieved by shifting the balance in favor of excitation, e.g. by blocking inhibition.
source: It is well–established that unstable states such as epileptiform activity can easily be achieved by shifting the balance in favor of excitation, e.g. by blocking inhibition (Dichter and Ayala, 1987; Bazhenov et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The concept of balanced excitation and inhibition was introduced two decades ago.
source: The concept of balanced excitation (E) and inhibition (I) (balanced networks in short) was introduced two decades ago (Shadlen and Newsome, 1994; van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996) and has sparked numerous studies both theoretical (Amit and Brunel, 1997; Ozeki et al., 2009; van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1998; Kumar et al., 2008) as well as experimental (Berg et al., 2007; Okun and Lampl, 2008; Higley and Contreras, 2006; Wehr and Zador, 2003; Kishore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the historical claim.

claim: The primary purpose of theoretical models of balanced networks was initially to understand irregular spiking.
source: The primary purpose of theoretical models of balanced networks was initially to understand irregular spiking, which was widely observed in experiments (Bell et al., 1995; Shadlen and Newsome, 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Irregular spiking was puzzling because it could not be explained by random arrival of excitatory input alone, since this randomness was effectively regularized by temporal integration.
source: Irregular spiking was puzzling because it could not be explained by random arrival of excitatory input alone, since this randomness was effectively regularized by temporal integration (Denève and Machens, 2016; Softky and Koch, 1993).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Models of balanced networks were able to explain irregular spiking.
source: Models of balanced networks not only were able to explain irregular spiking, but also revealed other interesting phenomena, such as emergent linearity (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996), multifunctionalism (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009; Hennequin et al., 2014) and self–sustained stable network activity (Amit and Brunel, 1997; Hansel and Mato, 2001; Ikegaya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Balanced network models revealed emergent linearity, multifunctionalism, and self-sustained stable network activity.
source: Models of balanced networks not only were able to explain irregular spiking, but also revealed other interesting phenomena, such as emergent linearity (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996), multifunctionalism (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009; Hennequin et al., 2014) and self–sustained stable network activity (Amit and Brunel, 1997; Hansel and Mato, 2001; Ikegaya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Irregular spiking results from a mean membrane potential lurking just below threshold, where it is restrained by inhibition concurrent with excitation.
source: The consensus view thus became that irregular spiking results from a mean membrane potential, which is lurking just below threshold, where it is restrained by inhibition concurrent with excitation (Shadlen and Newsome, 1998; Bell et al., 1995; Salinas and Sejnowski, 2000), although synchrony of random excitation is sometimes needed when individual synaptic potentials are small (Stevens and Zador, 1998).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Synchrony of random excitation is sometimes needed when individual synaptic potentials are small.
source: The consensus view thus became that irregular spiking results from a mean membrane potential, which is lurking just below threshold, where it is restrained by inhibition concurrent with excitation (Shadlen and Newsome, 1998; Bell et al., 1995; Salinas and Sejnowski, 2000), although synchrony of random excitation is sometimes needed when individual synaptic potentials are small (Stevens and Zador, 1998).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The concept of balanced E/I has been forgotten in understanding spinal motor networks, with the exception of a few isolated studies.
source: The concept of balanced E/I is now an integrated part of understanding network processing in cortex and elsewhere, but for some reason it has been forgotten in understanding spinal motor networks, with the exception of a few isolated studies (Berg et al., 2007; Petersen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Balanced E/I allows a subthreshold fluctuating membrane potential where spikes are evoked by synaptic transients in the fluctuation-driven regime.
source: The balanced E/I allow a subthreshold fluctuating membrane potential, where the spikes are evoked by synaptic transients and therefore belong to the fluctuation–driven regime (Kuhn et al., 2004; Tiesinga et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: In mean-driven spiking, the mean membrane potential is well above threshold and spike timing is controlled by after-hyperpolarization.
source: This is in contrast to the more traditional mean–driven spiking (Figure 1), where the mean membrane potential (Vm) is well above threshold and spike timing is controlled by after–hyperpolarization (Gerstner et al., 2014; Renart et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The fluctuation-driven regime has a skewed/lognormal firing rate distribution whereas the mean-driven regime has regular spiking and a symmetric distribution.
source: These two regimes have contrasting manifestations (Table 1): The fluctuation–driven regime has a skewed/lognormal firing rate distribution whereas the mean–driven regime has regular spiking and a symmetric distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Table 1.

claim: A simple mechanism has been proposed to explain the lognormal firing in the fluctuation-driven regime by Roxin et al. (2011): The skewness in distribution arises out of a supralinear transformation of the synaptic input, which is Gaussian by virtue of the central limit theorem.
source: A simple mechanism has been proposed to explain the lognormal firing in the fluctuation–driven regime by Roxin et al. (2011): The skewness in distribution arises out of a supralinear transformation of the synaptic input, which is Gaussian by virtue of the central limit theorem (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A supralinear response to multiple inputs will enhance sensitivity.
source: A response to multiple input, which is larger than the sum of their individual responses (i.e. supralinear), will enhance sensitivity (Rubin et al., 2015) and therefore this mechanism may constitute an important physiological purpose.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In the mean-driven regime, if the mean input is above threshold, the transformation is linear and the firing rate distribution is symmetric.
source: This is in contrast to the mean–driven regime where the summation is linear or even sublinear, which will transform a normally distributed input to a normally (as opposed to lognormally) distributed firing rate (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Linear or sublinear transformation in the mean-driven regime will reduce rather than enhance sensitivity and curb network activity.
source: Such linear (or sublinear) transformation will reduce rather than enhance sensitivity and therefore the mean–driven regime will curb network activity (Ahmadian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The two transformations work together into an S-shaped IO-curve, where weak input are amplified yet the network is kept stable for strong activity.
source: These two transformations work together into an S-shaped IO-curve, where weak input are amplified yet the network is kept stable for strong activity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The shape of the firing rate distribution reveals the spiking regime of a given neuron.
source: If this mechanism is true, then the shape of the firing rate distribution will reveal the spiking regime of a given neuron.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of the mechanism.

claim: The mechanical stability of the turtle preparation allows electrophysiological recordings of unprecedented quality.
source: The mechanical stability of the turtle preparation allows electrophysiological recordings of unprecedented quality, such that we can combine intracellular recording with multi–electrode arrays, and thus determine the fraction of the population in the two regimes at all times.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological advantage.

claim: The high resistance to anoxia of turtles allows using adult animals with fully developed spinal circuitry.
source: The high resistance to anoxia of turtles allows using adult animals with fully developed spinal circuitry, which have healthy network activity and which can perform multiple complex motor behaviors (Stein, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Custom designed high-density silicon electrodes recorded the population activity from hundreds of cells in the dorsoventral and rostrocaudal axes along with the intracellular Vm of single neurons and multiple relevant motor nerves.
source: Custom designed high–density silicon electrodes recorded the population activity from hundreds of cells in the dorsoventral and rostrocaudal axes along with the intracellular Vm of single neurons and multiple relevant motor nerves (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The parallel spiking activity of 200-300 single units were recorded in the medial to ventral horns of lumbar spinal segments involved in motor rhythm generation.
source: The parallel spiking activity of 200–300 single units were recorded in the medial to ventral horns of lumbar spinal segments involved in motor rhythm generation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The location of the electrode arrays in the ventral area of the lumbar enlargement was verified by histology.
source: The location of the electrode arrays in the ventral area of the lumbar enlargement was verified by histology (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Site-specific rhythmic hindlimb scratching was induced by tactile touch of the carapace.
source: Site–specific rhythmic hindlimb scratching was induced by tactile touch of the carapace (Berkowitz et al., 2010; Stein, 2005) and could be reproduced reliably over multiple trials (Petersen et al., 2014; Vestergaard and Berg, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The distribution of spike count firing rates across the population was skewed but resembled a normal distribution on logarithmic x-axis, i.e. a lognormal distribution.
source: The distribution of spike count firing rates across the population was skewned (Figure 2F), but resembled a normal distribution on logarithmic x-axis (inset), i.e. a lognormal distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 2F.

claim: Lognormal distributions could arise from a nonlinear transformation of normally distributed inputs.
source: Two mechanisms have previously been proposed to explain the skewned lognormal firing rate distribution, which is also observed in other parts of the nervous system (Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014). Lognormal distributions could either arise from a nonlinear transformation of normally distributed inputs (Roxin et al., 2011) (Figure 1A) or from a linear transformation of a lognormally distributed synaptic input (Wohrer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Lognormal distributions could arise from a linear transformation of a lognormally distributed synaptic input.
source: Two mechanisms have previously been proposed to explain the skewned lognormal firing rate distribution, which is also observed in other parts of the nervous system (Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014). Lognormal distributions could either arise from a nonlinear transformation of normally distributed inputs (Roxin et al., 2011) (Figure 1A) or from a linear transformation of a lognormally distributed synaptic input (Wohrer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Synaptic weights within neocortex have a heavy tail lognormal distribution rather than a Gaussian distribution.
source: The latter mechanism was considered in connection with the sparse spiking activity in auditory cortex (Koulakov et al., 2009; Hromádka et al., 2008) and since synaptic weights within neocortex have a heavy tail lognormal distribution rather than a Gaussian distribution (Ikegaya et al., 2013; Song et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The motor activity was clearly non-stationary, which means that the spike activity was likely to move between the fluctuation- and mean-regime.
source: The motor activity was clearly non–stationary, which means that the spike activity was likely to move between the fluctuation– and mean–regime.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the Results section.

claim: In the fluctuation-driven regime the conductance is often high and dominated by balanced E/I synaptic input.
source: This is likely justified for neurons in fluctuation–driven regime, since the conductance is often high and dominated by balanced E/I synaptic input (Destexhe et al., 2003; Kumar et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: A novel metric, the return map ratio, quantifies the degree of fluctuations leading up to a spike.
source: We therefore propose a novel metric, the return map ratio , which quantifies the degree of fluctuations leading up to a spike (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: An RMR close to 0.5 has fluctuation-driven spiking whereas a value close to 1 has mean-driven spiking.
source: An RMR close to 0.5 has fluctuation–driven spiking whereas a value close to 1 has mean–driven spiking (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A neuron was defined as fluctuation-driven if its RMR <0.7.
source: Therefore, we defined a neuron as fluctuation-driven if its RMR <0.7; in our sample of intracellular recordings we found 50/68 neurons in this regime.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological definition in the Results section.

claim: 50 out of 68 neurons were found in the fluctuation-driven regime based on the RMR metric.
source: Therefore, we defined a neuron as fluctuation-driven if its RMR <0.7; in our sample of intracellular recordings we found 50/68 neurons in this regime.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: The skewness for the Vm distributions across the population is small and scattered around zero as expected for normal (symmetric) distributions.
source: The skewness for the distributions across the population is small and scattered around zero as expected for normal (symmetric) distributions (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3E.

claim: The subthreshold Vm-distributions are not skewed, but rather symmetrical and Gaussian-like.
source: From these data we conclude that the subthreshold Vm–distributions are not skewed, but rather symmetrical and Gaussian–like (cf. inset distributions, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3E.

claim: Since the synaptic potentials are normally distributed, they are a result of a linear transformation of synaptic currents, which are also normally distributed.
source: A more parsimonious explanation therefore is that, since the synaptic potentials are normally distributed, they are a result of a linear transformation of synaptic currents, which are also normally distributed.
evidence: This is stated as an inference in the Results section.

claim: The IO-function had a strong non-linear shape.
source: The IO–function had a strong non–linear shape (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: The curvature of the IO-function had a weak negative correlation with the SD of the Vm-fluctuation.
source: To capture the curvature we fitted both a power–law and an exponential for all n=68 neurons and the curvature had a weak negative correlation with the SD of the Vm–fluctuation (Figure 4C–D) as demonstrated previously (Vestergaard and Berg, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Similar expansive nonlinearity has previously been characterized in sensory-driven neurons.
source: Similar expansive nonlinearity has previously been characterized in sensory–driven neurons (Anderson et al., 2000; Hansel and van Vreeswijk, 2002; Miller and Troyer, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The supralinear IO-function will transform the normally-distributed synaptic potentials into a lognormally-distributed spiking output in the fluctuation-driven regime.
source: It will transform the normally–distributed synaptic potentials into a lognormally–distributed spiking output in the fluctuation-driven regime (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: For mean-driven spiking the IO-function is not supralinear, but rather linear (or even sublinear), and the normally-distributed synaptic input will therefore be transformed to a normally distributed spiking output.
source: For mean–driven spiking the IO-function is not supralinear, but rather linear (or even sublinear), and the normally–distributed synaptic input will therefore be transformed to a normally distributed spiking output (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Neurons that have fluctuation-driven spiking also have a non-linear IO-transformation of synaptic potentials to spiking output.
source: In conclusion, neurons that have fluctuation–driven spiking also have a non–linear IO-transformation of synaptic potentials to spiking output.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section.

claim: The firing rate distribution of many cells was positively skewed and resembled a normal distribution with near zero skewness on a log-scale.
source: The firing rate distribution of many cells was positively skewed and resembled a normal distribution with near zero skewness on a log-scale (sample cell shown in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Lognormal firing rate distribution is expected for poisson-like spiking in the fluctuation-driven regime.
source: This is expected for poisson–like spiking in the fluctuation–driven regime (Ostojic, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Distributions for all the intracellularly recorded neurons (n=68) were skewed to a varying degree from strong positive to zero skewness on a linear axis.
source: Nevertheless, distributions for all the intracellularly recorded neurons (n=68) were skewed to a varying degree from strong positive to zero skewness on a linear axis and similarly shifted downwards on log axis (cf. gray and green histograms, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: Neurons were found in a spectrum between fluctuation- and mean-driven spiking.
source: This suggests that neurons were found in a spectrum between fluctuation– and mean–driven spiking.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section.

claim: More negative log-skewness were associated with higher mean rates.
source: More negative log–skewness were associated with higher mean rates (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: The subprimary range may have a more noteworthy role in covering the dynamical range in motor control than previously assumed.
source: This indicates that the fluctuation–regime may have a more noteworthy role in covering the dynamical range in motor control than previously assumed, which is in agreement with the observations of the present study.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: The skewness in firing rates is an indicator of the degree of participation in the fluctuation-driven regime.
source: In conclusion, these results suggest that the skewness in firing rates is an indicator of the degree of participation in the fluctuation–driven regime.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section.

claim: The fluctuation-driven neuron spent most of the time below threshold (96%).
source: Also, the cumulative time spent below threshold was higher for the fluctuation–driven cell (96%) than the mean–driven cell (35%, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 6D.

claim: The mean-driven neuron spent 35% of time below threshold.
source: Also, the cumulative time spent below threshold was higher for the fluctuation–driven cell (96%) than the mean–driven cell (35%, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 6D.

claim: Half of the population spent at least 84% of the time below threshold.
source: The intercept with the 50%–line (broken line) indicates what fraction of time half the population at least spent below threshold. This fraction is remarkably high (84%) suggesting a prominent presence within the fluctuation–driven regime.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 6E.

claim: A negative constant current injection (-1.0 nA) caused a decrease in firing rate and a slight increase in irregularity compared with zero injected current.
source: A negative constant current injection (−1.0 nA) caused a decrease in firing rate and a slight increase in irregularity (green line) compared with zero injected current (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 7A-B.

claim: A positive current injection (1.7 nA) caused more spikes and a decrease in irregularity.
source: Similarly, a positive current injection (1.7 nA) caused more spikes and a decrease in irregularity (Figure 7C) consistent with a movement between regimes (inset in Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 7C.

claim: The decrease in irregularity with increasing input was quantified as a negative correlation between mean CV2 and injected current (R=-0.84, p≪0.001) over multiple trials (n=18).
source: The decrease in irregularity with increasing input was further quantified as a negative correlation between mean C⁢V2 and injected current (R=-0.84, p≪0.001) over multiple trials (n=18, Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 7D.

claim: The instantaneous firing rate in the control condition (0 nA) was lognormal as expected for the fluctuation-driven regime.
source: The instantaneous firing rate in the control condition (0 nA) was lognormal as expected for the fluctuation–driven regime (top, Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 7E.

claim: When adding input current the distribution was shifted to the right and enriched with a negative skewness as expected for mean-driven spiking.
source: When adding input current the distribution was shifted to the right and enriched with a negative skewness as expected for mean-driven spiking (bottom, Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 7E.

claim: There was a negative correlation between multiple current injections and skewness both on linear scale (gray dots) and log-scale (red dots).
source: This relation between input and shape of rate distribution was further confirmed by a negative correlation between multiple current injections and skewness both on linear scale (gray dots) and log–scale (red dots, Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 7F.

claim: Skewness and irregularity are indicators of the spiking regime.
source: Hence, skewness and irregularity are indicators of the spiking regime.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section.

claim: Reducing inhibition tipped the balance of E/I toward larger inward synaptic current, which resulted in a more depolarized Vm well above threshold.
source: Reducing inhibition tipped the balance of E/I toward larger inward synaptic current, which resulted in a more depolarized Vm (blue line) well above threshold (arrows, Figure A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 8A-B.

claim: Blocking inhibition resulted in higher firing rates and lower irregularity on the peak.
source: It also resulted in higher firing rates and lower irregularity on the peak (cf. green lines).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The irregularity (CV2) was higher in the control case than in the unbalanced case.
source: Generally, the irregularity (C⁢V2) was higher in the control case than in the unbalanced case (Figure 8C) similar to the results observed with current injection (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: The irregularity was negatively correlated with depolarization of the mean Vm when unbalancing the E/I although it was uncorrelated in the control condition.
source: The irregularity was also negatively correlated with depolarization of the mean Vm when unbalancing the E/I although it was uncorrelated in the control condition, where the spiking occurred in the fluctuation–driven regime (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cumulative time spent below threshold was larger in the control condition (78%) compared with the unbalanced case (56%).
source: The cumulative time spent below threshold was larger in the control condition (78%) compared with the unbalanced case (56%, Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 8E.

claim: These observations are largely consistent with the consensus view that irregular fluctuation-driven spiking is due to a balance between excitation and inhibition.
source: These observations are largely consistent with the consensus view that irregular fluctuation–driven spiking is due to a balance between excitation and inhibition (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section.

claim: The neurons recorded with intracellular electrodes had more regular spiking than those recorded with extracellular electrodes.
source: We noticed a small difference in the distribution of irregularity among the neurons recorded with intracellular versus extracellular electrodes (data not shown). The neurons were recorded with intracellular electrodes had more regular spiking than those recorded with extracellular electrodes.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the Results section.

claim: There is an experimental bias towards high firing rates in intracellularly recorded neurons.
source: This may be caused by a systematic bias in the way the intracellularly recorded neurons were collected, as there is an experimental bias towards high firing rates.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation in the Results section.

claim: Spike sorting processing of the extracellular recordings is likely to both miss spikes and contain false positives, which will cause overestimation of spiking irregularity.
source: Spike sorting processing of the extracellular recordings, on the other hand, is likely to both miss spikes and contain false positives, which will cause overestimation of spiking irregularity.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation in the Results section.

claim: A randomness in the threshold had little or no effect on the irregularity of spiking compared with the randomness in synaptic input.
source: Therefore a randomness in the threshold had little of no effect on the irregularity of spiking compared with the randomness in synaptic input.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section.

claim: Neurons were active during both ipsi- and contralateral scratching behaviors.
source: Neurons were active during both ipsi– and contralateral scratching behaviors (Figure 9A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 9A-D.

claim: Most units had a rhythmic relationship with the nerve signals and a higher firing rate for the ipsilateral scratching compared with contralateral scratching behavior.
source: Most units had a rhythmic relationship with the nerve signals and a higher firing rate for the ipsilateral scratching compared with contralateral scratching behavior (cf. Figure 9C and D; Videos 1 and 2), which indicates participation of neurons in a hemicord to a smaller degree in the contralateral movement than the ipsilateral movement.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 9C-D and Videos 1-2.

claim: The distribution of firing rates across the neuronal population over several trials was strongly skewed, which indicate that most neurons spike relatively infrequently with a 'fat-tail' of higher spiking.
source: The distribution of firing rates across the neuronal population over several trials was strongly skewed, which indicate that most neurons spike relatively infrequently with a 'fat-tail' of higher spiking (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 9E.

claim: The distribution covered two orders of magnitudes from 0.1-10 Hz and was akin to a lognormal distribution.
source: The distribution covered two orders of magnitudes from 0.1–10 Hz and was akin to a lognormal distribution (inset and green lines, Figure 9E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 9E.

claim: Similar lognormal-like distributions have been observed in other parts of the nervous system.
source: Similar lognormal–like distributions have been observed in other parts of the nervous system (Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The firing rate distribution was positively skewed in both behaviors with the similar qualitative shape.
source: The firing rate distribution was positively skewed in both behaviors with the similar qualitative shape (Figure 9E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 9E-F.

claim: The skewness was found across animals (n=5) and close to zero on log-scale, i.e. lognormal.
source: This skewness was also found across animals (green bars, Figure 9G, n=5) and close to zero on log–scale, i.e. lognormal (black lower bars).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 9G.

claim: Although the mean firing rate could change between behaviors and between animals, the skewness was qualitatively similar.
source: Although the mean firing rate could change between behaviors and between animals (Figure 9J), the skewness was qualitatively similar (Figure 9K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 9J-K.

claim: The skewed lognormal-like firing rate distribution, and hence a presence of the fluctuation-driven regime, was preserved across behaviors and animals.
source: This suggests that the skewed lognormal–like firing rate distribution, and hence a presence of the fluctuation–driven regime, was preserved across behaviors and animals.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section.

claim: As the mean firing rate increased, the skewness of the distribution (log-scale) became negative, which is a sign of more neurons were occupying the mean-driven regime.
source: As the mean firing rate increased, the skewness of the distribution (log–scale) became negative, which is a sign of more neurons were occupying the mean–driven regime (cf. inset histograms, Figure 10A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 10A.

claim: There was a negative correlation between the mean firing rate and the log-skewness for all time points.
source: This was further confirmed by a negative correlation between the mean firing rate (black line in A) and the log–skewness for all time points (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 10B.

claim: As the general activity increased, the population distribution became less lognormal and more Gaussian, which suggests more neurons occupied the mean-driven regime during a higher general activity.
source: Hence, as the general activity increased, the population distribution became less lognormal and more Gaussian, which suggests more neurons occupied the mean–driven regime during a higher general activity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section.

claim: Both distributions of CV2 had substantial spread around the mean, which suggests a rich diversity spiking patterns.
source: Both distributions had substantial spread around the mean, which suggests a rich diversity spiking patterns.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section.

claim: Half of the population spent at least 58% of time in the fluctuation regime during ipsilateral scratching.
source: Hence, half of the population spent at least 58% of time in the fluctuation regime during ipsilateral scratching (intercept of curve with the broken line, Figure 10D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 10D.

claim: During development, a distinct laminar organization of different cellular subtypes is formed in the dorsoventral axis.
source: During development, a distinct laminar organization of different cellular subtypes is formed in the dorsoventral axis (Arber, 2012; Jessell, 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Motoneurons are primarily found in the most ventral part of the horn whereas interneurons are found in more medial to dorsal territory.
source: In particular, motoneurons are primarily found in the most ventral part of the horn whereas interneurons are found in more medial to dorsal territory.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The distributions of mean firing rates and the mean CV2 had no obvious dependence on depth.
source: The distributions of mean firing rates (not shown) and the mean C⁢V2 (Figure 11E) had no obvious dependence on depth.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 11E.

claim: The spread in means of CV2 was much smaller than the SD of the distributions themselves.
source: In particular, the spread in means was much smaller than the SD of the distributions themselves.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The fluctuation-driven spiking regime was both present and equally prominent in all the neurons, regardless of whether the cell body was in the ventral horn or in the medial horn, i.e. equally present in motoneurons and interneurons.
source: The most parsimonious interpretation of these data is that the fluctuation–driven spiking regime was both present and equally prominent in all the neurons, regardless of whether the cell body was in the ventral horn or in the medial horn, i.e. equally present in motoneurons and interneurons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section.

claim: This is the first report which quantifies occupation within spiking regimes of a neuronal population, not just in the spinal cord, but also in the nervous system in general.
source: To our knowledge this is the first report, which quantifies occupation within spiking regimes of a neuronal population, not just in the spinal cord, but also in the nervous system in general.
evidence: This is stated as a claim of novelty in the Discussion section.

claim: The prominent presence of the fluctuation-regime implies that the majority of neuronal spikes were not driven primarily by intrinsic properties such as pacemaker potentials, but rather by synaptic communication.
source: The prominent presence of the fluctuation–regime therefore implies that the majority of neuronal spikes were not driven primarily by intrinsic properties such as pacemaker potentials, but rather by synaptic communication.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: If there is a pacemaker-driven rhythmogenic core of oscillatory neurons responsible for the motor activity, the core only represents a small fraction of the network.
source: This can be interpreted in two ways: (1) if there is a pacemaker–driven rhythmogenic core of oscillatory neurons responsible for the motor activity (Huckstepp et al., 2016), the core only represents a small fraction of the network, or (2) since the fluctuation–regime is prominent and pacemaker neurons are difficult to find, the motor–rhythm may be generated by other means such as emergent collective processes in the network (Yuste, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a possible interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: The motor-rhythm may be generated by emergent collective processes in the network rather than pacemaker neurons.
source: This can be interpreted in two ways: (1) if there is a pacemaker–driven rhythmogenic core of oscillatory neurons responsible for the motor activity (Huckstepp et al., 2016), the core only represents a small fraction of the network, or (2) since the fluctuation–regime is prominent and pacemaker neurons are difficult to find, the motor–rhythm may be generated by other means such as emergent collective processes in the network (Yuste, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a possible interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: Generation of movements without the need of pacemaker neurons have been predicted theoretically in central pattern generators.
source: Generation of movements without the need of pacemaker neurons have been predicted theoretically in central pattern generators (Kleinfeld and Sompolinsky, 1988) as well as more complex sequence generation (Hennequin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Even in the respiratory system, which has the most stereotypic motor rhythm, pacemaker cells appear not to be essential for generation of the rhythmic breathing, although this topic is still debated.
source: Even in the respiratory system, which has the most stereotypic motor rhythm, pacemaker cells appear not to be essential for generation of the rhythmic breathing, although this topic is still debated (Feldman et al., 2013; Ramirez et al., 2011; Carroll and Ramirez, 2013; Chevalier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: This report is the first investigation of spinal motor circuits from an ensemble viewpoint.
source: To the best of our knowledge this report is the first investigation of spinal motor circuits from an ensemble viewpoint.
evidence: This is stated as a claim of novelty in the Discussion section.

claim: The fraction of motoneurons to interneurons is 1:8.
source: The fraction of motoneurons to interneurons is 1:8 (Walloe et al., 2011), but we were also likely to sample motorneurons, since they have large somata.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Similar irregularity is observed in invertebrates.
source: Similar irregularity is observed in invertebrates (Bruno et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The distribution of mean CV2 values is more regular than what is observed for typical cortical neurons but similar to cervical interneurons in monkeys performing isometric wrist flexion-extensions.
source: This is more regular than what is observed for typical cortical neurons (although see Feng and Brown, 1999), but similar to cervical interneurons in monkeys performing isometric wrist flexion–extensions (Prut and Perlmutter, 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The subprimary range accounts for 90% of the contraction force in motoneurons.
source: Nevertheless, a recent study recorded for the first time the motoneuron discharge and muscle force and found that the subprimary range accounts for 90% of the contraction force (Manuel and Heckman, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The surgical procedures comply with Danish legislation and were approved by the controlling body under the Ministry of Justice.
source: The surgical procedures comply with Danish legislation and were approved by the controlling body under the Ministry of Justice.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
